power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Innovative and accessible strategies are needed to address mental health burden among university students.
Nature-based interventions (NBIs), which involve therapeutic activities conducted in nature spaces, are emerging to promote student wellbeing on university campuses.
This review examined the range of NBIs implemented within universities and their reported benefits using a systematic search and narrative synthesis methodology.
Evidence was searched from database inception to August 2026, identifying twelve studies representing eleven trials across five countries.
Interventions involved forest therapy (n=5), mindfulness-based programs (n=4) adapted for outdoor campus settings, and therapeutic horticulture interventions (n=3).
Evidence suggests that forest therapy is associated with reductions in stress and anxiety and improvements in mood, attention and overall wellbeing.
Nature-integrated mindfulness programs were linked to reduced depressive symptoms, rumination, stress and anxiety, alongside enhanced wellbeing, mindfulness and connection to nature.

Preliminary evidence suggests on campus therapeutic horticulture interventions may be associated with improvements in anxiety among university students and represent an accessible and affordable way to build nature and social connection.
While findings are promising, evidence remains limited and of weak quality, highlighting the need for further robust research on implementation and sustainability within university contexts.

text.text: A systematic and comprehensive search strategy was developed using Boolean logic (AND/OR) including a combination of key terms and database-specific subject headings (e.g.
MESH terms) to identify studies examining the application of NBIs within university campus settings.
The following electronic databases were searched: MEDLINE Complete (EBSCO), PsycINFO (EBSCO), Embase (OVID), CINAHL (EBSCO) and Cochrane Central (NMHRC).
Search terms were organised into two major categories: NBIs and university populations (see Supplementary Materials A for full search strategy).
Eligibility criteria were defined a priori according to the PICOS framework (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes, and Study Design).
The population of interest was enrolled university students.
Interventions included NBIs delivered on general university campus grounds.
Studies were required to report one or more psychological wellbeing outcomes.
Studies of any design that were published in English were eligible for inclusion.
Non-peer-reviewed studies and other grey literature were excluded.
Searches were initially conducted in 2023 using Covidence (Version 2) and subsequently updated in 2025 and August 2026 to identify newly published literature.

For the search in 2023, following the removal of duplicate records, two reviewers (CZ and NH) independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, with disagreements resolved through discussion and, where necessary, consultation with a third reviewer (MOS).
Full-text articles were then retrieved and independently assessed for eligibility by the same two reviewers.
The authors of three identified records were contacted to clarify aspects relevant to eligibility (e.g., whether studies used the same or different participant pools).

Records identified through the 2025 and 2026 search updates were screened independently by HC and KG using the same eligibility criteria and review procedures and were incorporated into the review where eligible.
For all searches, any disagreements were reviewed by MOS, who made the final determination regarding inclusion.
Reference lists of key reviews (e.g. He et al., 2024) were also hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies not identified through the database search strategy.

text.text: Quality scores were assigned based on six categories: selection bias, study design, confounders, blinding, data collection methods, and withdrawals and dropouts.
The assessment was performed by one reviewer (SM or KG) and verified by a second (MC or HC).

Data were extracted by one reviewer and checked for accuracy by a second reviewer according to the following study characteristics: (i) authors/date/country of publication, (ii) aims, (iii) study design, (iv) sample information, (v) intervention information, (vi) scales/measures used, (vii) outcomes and main findings, (viii) limitations and (ix) quality appraisal.
Data were then examined according to the key research questions, with a focus on the types and wellbeing outcomes of NBIs being delivered on university campuses globally.
A narrative synthesis was then undertaken to provide an integrated interpretation of the findings and guide future research and implementation.
The search strategy yielded 1212 records after duplicates were removed.
Following title and abstract screening, 67 studies were identified for full-text review, of which 56 were excluded based on the selection criteria.

Main reasons for exclusion included a focus on nature exposure alone (including walking interventions without associated therapeutic activities), rather than the implementation of a prescribed NBI (e.g., Ballew & Omoto, 2018; Shrestha et al., 2021); an NBI being delivered for students off-campus (e.g., Djernis et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2024); the intervention being delivered in connection with a Forestry, rather than a general university campus (e.g., Yang et al., 2024); or due to ineligible study type (e.g., Vitagliano et al., 2023; protocol paper).

text.text: The primary methodological limitations were consistent across studies: most relied on self-selected samples of university students and participation rates were rarely reported.
While study design was typically rated as moderate, descriptions of randomisation were poorly detailed, and confounders were generally uncontrolled and not assessed at baseline.
Given the nature of NBIs, participants were aware of their intervention status; outcome assessors were also typically not blinded to participants status (with the exception of Owens & Bunce, 2022).

text.text: This review aimed to identify and critically appraise existing evidence on the use of NBIs within university campus settings.
Although interest in campus greenspace NBIs is growing, we found that research in this area remains limited, with only twelve studies identified.

Approximately half of these studies explored the benefits of on-campus forest therapy at a single university, while a small majority focused on mindfulness-based programs -traditionally delivered indoors -that were adapted for outdoor campus environments, and two studies assessed therapeutic horticulture interventions in campus garden spaces.

Collectively, the findings suggest that NBIs may offer meaningful mental health benefits for university students, but further evidence is required to understand their feasibility and value within higher education settings.

Our review identified two primary forms of NBIs currently employed as part of university greenspace wellbeing initiatives, identifying these as potentially feasible approaches for future implementation: (1) forest therapy and (2) mindfulness-based interventions adapted for outdoor campus settings.

The review also identified a potential for therapeutic horticultural activities to support university students in campus garden spaces, where mindfulness is identified as a key component (Pantiru et al., 2024).

text.text: Overall, the findings suggest that students engaging in on-campus forest therapy reported significant reductions in stress and anxiety, alongside improvements in attention, mood and overall psychological wellbeing.
This aligns with recent reviews that suggest that forest therapy may be particularly beneficial for young people (Pavlovic & Connolly, 2023), including university students (e.g., He et al., 2024).

text.text: Additionally, students engaging in nature-integrated mindfulness programs reported improvements in a range of outcomes, including reduced depressive symptoms, rumination, anxiety and stress, as well as enhanced wellbeing, energy, mindfulness and nature connection.

These findings reflect recent evidence demonstrating that mindfulness-based interventions can improve psychological wellbeing among university students and reduce levels of anxiety, depression and rumination (Dawson et al., 2020; González-Martín et al., 2023; Johnson et al., 2023).

text.text: Across the included studies, the duration of NBIs varied, ranging from brief single-session formats (one to 20 minutes) to longer duration multi-session interventions (up to 2 hours).
Given the small number of studies, specific recommendations regarding the optimal length or duration of campus-based NBIs cannot yet be made.

Nevertheless, the overall acceptability of NBIs reported by students across all included studies encourages future examination of both their benefits and implementation factors that might support greater uptake within university settings and across more diverse groups of students.

text.text: Given the rising rates of climate distress and anxiety among university students (Cameron & Kagee, 2025; Tavolacci & Ladner, 2024), an expansion of research into the role of NBIs within whole-of-university student mental health and wellbeing strategies is strongly recommended.

text.text: While aimed at providing a comprehensive appraisal of the use of NBIs in the higher education sector, this review is limited by the number of studies identified.

Included studies were concentrated within a small number of universities, with almost half conducted at a single institution in South Korea, thereby limiting the potential generalisability of findings.
No studies were conducted in Australia.
Additionally, the methodological quality of included studies was rated as weak overall, with a general lack of controlled studies published to date.
Grey literature was not explored, which means that potentially other campus-based NBIs or relevant implementation recommendations were not identified.
In addition, several studies that may offer notable perspectives were outside the scope of this review.

For example, several studies have examined the outcomes of NBIs conducted in nature settings adjacent or nearby to, rather than within, university campuses (e.g., Djernis et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2024), while others have examined the psychological benefits of general exposure to on-campus green spaces but did not conduct a NBI so were not included (e.g., Shrestha et al., 2021).

text.text: The growing mental health burden among university students highlights the need for innovative, accessible wellbeing strategies.

This review provides preliminary support for broadening greenspace initiatives -specifically forest therapy, nature-based mindfulness and therapeutic horticulture interventions -as part of a more comprehensive and holistic university mental health strategy.
Situated within the university environment, these programs may be especially accessible to university students and account for their various academic, social and extracurricular demands.

When delivered in campus settings, NBIs may also contribute to the environmental sustainability of universities and promote their roles in addressing the health challenges associated with urbanisation.
Increased uptake of NBIs is called for, alongside future research that focuses on optimising their design, acceptability, feasibility and sustainability within the university context.

Our author team comprises researchers and practitioners from Deakin University spanning Psychology, Health and Social Development, Exercise and Nutrition Sciences, Architecture and Built Environment, Diversity Equity and Inclusion and Student Services.
Together, we bring cross-disciplinary expertise and a shared commitment to improving student mental health and wellbeing.

Our work is united by a belief that universities can play a vital role in easing mental health burden for our students through the thoughtful design, care and activation of campus greenspaces that foster nature connection and support the integration of evidence-informed nature-based interventions.
